For that, the Centre for Effective Altruism’s post by @Tess Newton-Palmer on how to talk about the other FTX series, Netflix’s The Altruists (quite a month for TV shows on this topic) may be more useful for you. 


TL;DR: Effective altruism is at the heart of most of the first episode. The series seems to aim at reflecting reality without painting a very negative picture of EA. It shows that earning to give is what led Sam into this sector, and also that some of the effective altruists who worked with him early on, Tara Mac Aulay in particular, pushed for more prudence and for keeping promises to investors. Over the first two episodes, Sam comes across increasingly as a gambler, more and more detached from his initial altruistic goals.

What I took from the episodes: the gambler and the EAs who pushed back

The series presents Sam as a utilitarian loner and gambler inspired by earning to give, but it also lets other voices inspired by effective altruism be heard.

Earning to give at the root of the story

My view is that the series doesn’t stray far from reality. Even though effective altruism is mostly seen through the lens of earning to give, it is directly what led Sam into this sector. The documentary leans quite heavily on EA, with several excerpts from EA conference talks, notably by Will MacAskill, whose role in Sam’s path is well documented.

There is also the testimony of Tara Mac Aulay, former CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism and co-founder of Alameda Research. Even though she helped Sam get into crypto and co-founded the company with him, I’d say she represents effective altruism well, because she is clearly one of the sane and ethical people featured in the documentary. She explains the disagreements over risk management and business ethics, and what led her to leave.

The documentary doesn’t paint the worst possible picture of SBF (I was surprised by some of the choices, which, to me, cast a somewhat a neutral, or even somewhat positive, light on someone who committed such a massive fraud). It begins with his childhood and includes testimony from his parents. Sam also describes his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy. It also builds a narrative of Sam as a very isolated person who makes extremely dangerous decisions.

Some members of the EA community worked for Sam in the early days. As the series tells it, the initial motivations are clear: these are very altruistic people, Sam included. After the split, the company turns more and more towards people willing to take risks. Most of the new hires were not looking to have an impact; they just wanted to get rich. While the first people involved were, perhaps, altruists, FTX became a money-maximising operation.

Sam keeps reasoning in terms of expected value, for instance arguing that a 20% chance of FTX not being a flop is enough to justify it. Yet none of the people depicted as effective altruists in the series makes this kind of argument, and by then most of the early ones have left. In a way, they come across as the voice of reason. Through Tara’s voice, effective altruism is associated with prudence and with the importance of keeping promises and not deceiving people.

Over the two episodes, Sam goes further and further in pursuit of more money, more profit, without starting to give significantly, and seems more and more detached from any altruistic goal. My personal impression is of a gambler going double or nothing every three months; what the series shows is Sam’s growing delusions of grandeur. The series also points out how little was donated compared with the company’s valuation, criticises the investment in a coal-powered mine on climate grounds, and shows the money spent on advertising. In the show’s narrative, all of this seems tied to the delusions of grandeur Sam develops as the episodes go on.

The relationship with Caroline

His relationship with Caroline Ellison is at the heart of the second episode. The episode ends with the first signs of trouble in Alameda’s management: the firm relies mostly on its own assets, which are far too unstable.

This summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI.

item.title: Where I Am Donating in 2026
item.description:
Published on November 16, 2026 9:29 PM GMT

I didn't want to spend 200 hours deciding where to donate like I did last year. Therefore, there are some promising orgs that I did not take the time to learn more about, and this writeup doesn't provide as much detail as 2024 or 2025. But I'll try to cover the big stuff.

Cross-posted from my website.

Cause prioritization

I explained my thinking in detail in 2024, and some changes to my beliefs in 2025. My high-level prioritization has not changed in 2026:

  • The top priority is to prevent misaligned AI from killing everyone.
  • The best way to do that is a global halt on frontier AI development.
  • At the margin, the best things to do are public and political advocacy to push for a global halt.

Since 2025, I've written some posts that add color to my views, including:

  • I'm extremely worried that superintelligent AI will kill everyone — the basic case for why I care about AI risk. Not a new belief, but it's the first time I've straightforwardly put it into writing.
  • Worlds where we solve AI alignment on purpose don't look like the world we live in — a collection of reasons why things look grim.
  • Pausing AI Is the Best Answer to Post-Alignment Problems — even if we solve alignment, there are a lot of ways the future could go badly; a moratorium on superintelligence seems like the best response.

(There are more relevant posts in the archive, especially under the "Existential Risk" and "Far Future" headings.)

A lot happened since last year, but not much that changed my priorities

This year:

  • Frontier AI has made huge improvements on certain cognitive tasks like math, even solving a Millennium Prize problem.
  • Anthropic's AI systems may be significantly accelerating its AI R&D, which suggests we may be on the brink of recursive self-improvement. We may be very close to the point of no return.
  • The Hugging Face incident was the first (and possibly last) "warning shot", where an AI system went rogue and caused real-world damage. The incident woke a lot of people up to the dangers of advanced AI.
  • Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, and his resignation went unexpectedly viral and received a lot of media attention.

This all matters a lot, but it doesn't really change my prioritization. Here's how it did change my beliefs:

  • I have higher credence that pausing AI is urgent.
  • I'm more optimistic about our chances of achieving a global moratorium on AI development—the issue is both more popular and more salient.[1]
  • I'm less optimistic that things will miraculously work out somehow (e.g., it turns out alignment is easy, all you have to do is pick the right model persona or whatever). The window for a miracle is rapidly closing, and we're getting increasing evidence that current alignment techniques are not going to work.

Basically, 2026 has made me more confident in my preferred strategy of "advocate for a global ban on ASI".

There are more orgs working toward that goal (and doing advocacy toward that goal) than there were a year ago, but still not many orgs, so the cause remains neglected.

Post-alignment problems remain under-rated, but I don't see standout funding opportunities

By "post-alignment problems", I refer to the existential-scale problems that AI could bring even if we solve the alignment problem. Achieving an ideal future requires solving some critical problems, and it's not at all obvious that these problems can be deferred to AI.

Pausing AI is the best answer to post-alignment problems, but not necessarily the most cost-effective thing to work on.

  • I'm pessimistic about most relevant research agendas—I explained why in We won't solve post-alignment problems by doing research.

  • I'd like to see more work on post-ASI non-human welfare; I wrote about this here. There are a few orgs working on this and they get very little funding right now. However, I'm concerned that none of them take ASI sufficiently seriously, and their strategies will not scale to ASI (see The Future Will Be Weirder Than That).

  • Orgs like Compassion Aligned Machine Learning (CaML) work to improve AI's concern for sentient welfare. Will that work scale to superintelligence? I'm pretty sure it won't, and even if it does, it's difficult to imagine a world where this sort of work would make a difference (which is the point I made in An ASI that's bad for animal welfare is probably bad for humans, too). However, my reasoning could be wrong. I still think CaML-style work is a good expected-value bet because it's so underfunded—but maybe not as good a bet as AI pause advocacy.

  • I don't know what kind of work will improve sentient welfare post-ASI, given that we have no clue what an aligned ASI would look like. This is something I've been thinking about a lot and want to write more about soon. As for how this affects my donations, I don't see any orgs in the space who have good ideas about this, or who appear on track to come up with good ideas, so there's no one I clearly want to fund to work on the problem. For my preliminary thoughts on the problem, see:

    • I used to think aligned ASI would be good for all sentient beings; now I don't know what to think
    • An ASI that's bad for animal welfare is probably bad for humans, too

    (I realize these titles sound contradictory; that's because the subject is confusing and I'm not sure what I think. But the two posts' content are basically consistent with each other.)

  • Perhaps the goal of "get ASI to care about non-human welfare" is insufficiently general, and really the goal should be "solve ethics", or perhaps something like "achieve perfect strategic competence, and then follow the optimal strategy"[2] (see writings by Wei Dai: 1, 2, 3). But what org do I donate to in that case? Wei Dai is way ahead of the curve on thinking about philosophical competence, and more people should follow in his footsteps. There are a lot of people thinking about moral philosophy and the problem of solving ethics, but it's not clear what kinds of thinking are useful.

The #1 item on my research agenda is to reduce my confusion about post-alignment problems, especially non-human welfare. And it's plausible that some work in this space is more important at the margin than AI pause advocacy. But I don't currently see any funding opportunities that stand out as a clear priority in the way that AI pause advocacy stands out.[3]

Organizations (tax-deductible)

There are a few other protest orgs or public advocacy orgs that I didn't list, but not because I dislike anything about them; it's just that I don't know anything about them. Some possible contenders that I know very little about include People for a Pause, Humans in Control, and Irreplaceable. I believe the last two of those are less focused on extinction risk and more about the negative economic impacts of AI, but I'm not sure.

Evitable

Evitable is a new org that does public advocacy for a global moratorium on ASI. They do grassroots organizing—they've been involved in protests and done some preliminary movement-building, and they plan to do more kinds of mobilization in the future. They also make public content on AI risk, including appearing in various national news outlets.

A big component of my decision process is: find writings (or interviews, etc.) by the leader of an org and see how reasonable they sound. Do they understand the AI risk situation? Do they understand why alignment is hard? Are they focusing on the right things? Evitable gets big points because their founder David Krueger scores exceptionally well on the reasonableness test. I read some of his news articles and LessWrong posts and found myself cheering along with everything he said.

Evitable has more expertise on AI and AI alignment than the other grassroots advocacy orgs—David Krueger is an Assistant Professor in Machine Learning and has co-authored numerous AI safety papers; he and Gretchen Krueger (also at Evitable) are co-authors on the recent paper The Feasibility of a Hardwired Pause of Frontier AI Training. This sort of expertise isn't a requirement for running an advocacy org, but it's a nice bonus.

Evitable hasn't done much yet. I talked to them about their plans, and I'm reasonably confident that they will make good tradeoffs about what directions to pursue. A downside of their approach (focusing on capacity-building first) is that AI timelines may be very short, and their efforts might not pay off in time.

Lightcone Infrastructure

Lightcone Infrastructure takes AI risk seriously, and they do various projects that they expect to improve the situation. They mainly build community support and infrastructure, including running LessWrong, the Lighthaven event venue, and (more recently) creating the philanthropy platform Lightcone Commons.

Lightcone leadership is strategically and organizationally competent. The org is good enough to make my short list, but it's difficult to weigh the marginal value of community infrastructure against more direct public advocacy. My vibe sense is I prefer advocacy.

There's a conflict of interest in that I was paid by Lightcone Infrastructure to do some work this year, but at that point I was already pretty sure I wasn't going to donate to them.

Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)

If MIRI had no money, it would be a strong contender for the best place to donate. However, the other orgs on my list are funding-constrained to a degree that MIRI isn't. I really, really want Nate Soares and Eliezer Yudkowsky to keep raising the alarm about AI risk, but there is no danger that MIRI runs out of money and they stop being able to do that. The marginal things MIRI can do with funding are still good, but probably not as good as some of the other orgs on my short list.

Palisade Research

Palisade isn't my 2nd favorite org on this list,[4] but it's the one where I was 2nd most likely to donate—I liked Evitable more than the other grassroots advocacy orgs, Palisade is doing something different (see my 2024 summary), and I was uncertain about which approach was better. I decided I still prefer to donate to grassroots advocacy, the same as in 2024 and 2025.

The main update on Palisade is that in 2024, they had mostly done technical work and were just starting to scale up their political advocacy. Now, in 2026, they have been actively doing political advocacy, and I like what I've seen from them (although I don't know a lot of details).

PauseAI Global

PauseAI Global organizes protests outside of the US. As I wrote in 2024, I support their work, but I prefer to donate to US-based orgs because I believe US AI policy matters much more than policy in any other country.

As of November 2026, their website directs US readers to People for a Pause. This suggests that, if I like PauseAI Global, I should donate to People for a Pause. I decided not to donate to People for a Pause because I know more about Evitable and Stop the AI Race and I trust the latter orgs more.

I have two concerns about PauseAI Global based on private information. The first is a minor concern that I know to be true; the second is a medium-to-large concern, but I don't know whether it's accurate. I would prefer not to make vague statements like this, but unfortunately that is the situation. I would probably still donate to PauseAI Global if they were the only org doing protests.

PauseAI US

I talked about why I liked PauseAI US in 2024 and 2025. One positive update is that PauseAI US now spends more time coordinating volunteers' meetings with policy-makers across the country, which is a great thing to do.

A lot of people in AI safety take issue with the fact that PauseAI US's director, Holly Elmore, behaves antagonistically toward many people on Twitter, especially AI company employees. I don't spiritually object to this. Most safety work at AI companies is safetywashing, papering over misalignment, or contributing more to capabilities than to safety; the people doing those things should stop. That doesn't necessarily mean you should call them out personally in public. I'm not overly concerned that Holly is violating some important norm; if anyone's violating norms, it's the people working at AI companies. I've heard some accuse Holly of dishonesty, but the statements being pointed to as dishonest strike me as more like biased or motivated.[5] (Here is my Twitter reply to one specific claim.)

Sometimes Holly criticizes AI safety people who (in my view) are doing good work, but have associations with AI companies. I think that's going too far, although I see where she's coming from.[6]

I am concerned that many people dislike Holly's Twitter presence. It creates two problems:

  1. It gives many people a bad impression of the AI pause movement.
  2. It makes some other orgs unwilling to work with PauseAI US, which makes cooperation harder—this is important for organizing protests, etc.

Is it strategically useful to be antagonistic on Twitter? Holly says yes; I lean toward no, although I don't have a strong view.

Last year, I was concerned about the downside risk, but I believed it was outweighed by PauseAI US's activities on things I liked: protests, messaging campaigns, organizing meetings between policy-makers and concerned citizens. And there wasn't anyone else doing all those things. I have become more concerned about the downside risk since then, and there are more people organizing protests and grassroots support than there were a year ago. Therefore, this year I'd rather donate to Evitable or Stop the AI Race, although I still believe the more extreme criticisms of PauseAI US are overstated.

Stop the AI Race

Stop the AI Race It co-organized a large SF protest earlier this year. Before that, the org's founder, Michaël Trazzi, did a hunger strike against DeepMind. I'm impressed by his agency and dedication, and I like what I've seen so far.

There isn't much info available about Stop the AI Race. Even though the org is a strong candidate, I decided not to investigate further because I wasn't sure what information would convince me to donate. It comes down to who I trust more to execute well; Stop the AI Race looks promising on that front, but right now I trust Evitable more, and I don't know how to get good information other than just waiting and seeing who gets more traction.

Organizations (non-tax-deductible)

Last year, I didn't write much about non-tax-deductible orgs; I just said I'd investigate more later. I ended up not doing much investigation, but I ruled out donating to most 501(c)(4)s. My issues with most of them are:

  • Their preferred policies don't look like they'd have a big enough impact on extinction risk.
  • They're cagey about talking about extinction risk, and I don't trust them to share my priorities.

I did talk to them a bit, but I'm concerned that they are sufficiently politically savvy that they know how to make it sound to me like they share my priorities even when they actually don't.[7]

There are two exceptions for 501(c)(4)s that I consider sufficiently well-aligned: ControlAI and Encode AI.

By MichaelDickens

Published on November 16, 2026 9:29 PM GMT

I didn't want to spend 200 hours deciding where to donate like I did last year. Therefore, there are some promising orgs that I did not take the time to learn more about, and this writeup doesn't provide as much detail as 2024 or 2025. But I'll try to cover the big stuff.

Cross-posted from my website.

Cause prioritization

I explained my thinking in detail in 2024, and some changes to my beliefs in 2025. My high-level prioritization has not changed in 2026:

  • The top priority is to prevent misaligned AI from killing everyone.
  • The best way to do that is a global halt on frontier AI development.
  • At the margin, the best things to do are public and political advocacy to push for a global halt.

Since 2025, I've written some posts that add color to my views, including:

  • I'm extremely worried that superintelligent AI will kill everyone — the basic case for why I care about AI risk. Not a new belief, but it's the first time I've straightforwardly put it into writing.
  • Worlds where we solve AI alignment on purpose don't look like the world we live in — a collection of reasons why things look grim.
  • Pausing AI Is the Best Answer to Post-Alignment Problems — even if we solve alignment, there are a lot of ways the future could go badly; a moratorium on superintelligence seems like the best response.

(There are more relevant posts in the archive, especially under the "Existential Risk" and "Far Future" headings.)

A lot happened since last year, but not much that changed my priorities

This year:

  • Frontier AI has made huge improvements on certain cognitive tasks like math, even solving a Millennium Prize problem.
  • Anthropic's AI systems may be significantly accelerating its AI R&D, which suggests we may be on the brink of recursive self-improvement. We may be very close to the point of no return.
  • The Hugging Face incident was the first (and possibly last) "warning shot", where an AI system went rogue and caused real-world damage. The incident woke a lot of people up to the dangers of advanced AI.
  • Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, and his resignation went unexpectedly viral and received a lot of media attention.

This all matters a lot, but it doesn't really change my prioritization. Here's how it did change my beliefs:

  • I have higher credence that pausing AI is urgent.
  • I'm more optimistic about our chances of achieving a global moratorium on AI development—the issue is both more popular and more salient.[1]
  • I'm less optimistic that things will miraculously work out somehow (e.g., it turns out alignment is easy, all you have to do is pick the right model persona or whatever). The window for a miracle is rapidly closing, and we're getting increasing evidence that current alignment techniques are not going to work.

Basically, 2026 has made me more confident in my preferred strategy of "advocate for a global ban on ASI".

There are more orgs working toward that goal (and doing advocacy toward that goal) than there were a year ago, but still not many orgs, so the cause remains neglected.

Post-alignment problems remain under-rated, but I don't see standout funding opportunities

By "post-alignment problems", I refer to the existential-scale problems that AI could bring even if we solve the alignment problem. Achieving an ideal future requires solving some critical problems, and it's not at all obvious that these problems can be deferred to AI.

Pausing AI is the best answer to post-alignment problems, but not necessarily the most cost-effective thing to work on.

  • I'm pessimistic about most relevant research agendas—I explained why in We won't solve post-alignment problems by doing research.

  • I'd like to see more work on post-ASI non-human welfare; I wrote about this here. There are a few orgs working on this and they get very little funding right now. However, I'm concerned that none of them take ASI sufficiently seriously, and their strategies will not scale to ASI (see The Future Will Be Weirder Than That).

  • Orgs like Compassion Aligned Machine Learning (CaML) work to improve AI's concern for sentient welfare. Will that work scale to superintelligence? I'm pretty sure it won't, and even if it does, it's difficult to imagine a world where this sort of work would make a difference (which is the point I made in An ASI that's bad for animal welfare is probably bad for humans, too). However, my reasoning could be wrong. I still think CaML-style work is a good expected-value bet because it's so underfunded—but maybe not as good a bet as AI pause advocacy.

  • I don't know what kind of work will improve sentient welfare post-ASI, given that we have no clue what an aligned ASI would look like. This is something I've been thinking about a lot and want to write more about soon. As for how this affects my donations, I don't see any orgs in the space who have good ideas about this, or who appear on track to come up with good ideas, so there's no one I clearly want to fund to work on the problem. For my preliminary thoughts on the problem, see:

    • I used to think aligned ASI would be good for all sentient beings; now I don't know what to think
    • An ASI that's bad for animal welfare is probably bad for humans, too

    (I realize these titles sound contradictory; that's because the subject is confusing and I'm not sure what I think. But the two posts' content are basically consistent with each other.)

item.title: We’re a new charity evaluator. Our first recommendation: Raising The Village
item.description:
Published on November 17, 2026 12:21 PM GMT

We’re the co-founders of Better Futures Guide (BFG), a charity evaluator specifically focused on livelihoods. We were founded last year through Ambitious Impact’s Charity Entrepreneurship Incubation Program. We welcome questions, criticism and opportunities for collaboration, in the comments or at info@betterfuturesguide.org.

Summary

  • Better Futures Guide is a new charity evaluator focused on livelihoods: programs that work with people living in poverty to increase their incomes and what they can provide for themselves and their families. Our research and recommendations are public.
  • Our first recommendation is in "poverty graduation”,  an approach that gives households a bundle of support for roughly 1-2 years, on the premise that households are more likely to exit extreme poverty in a durable way when several of their constraints are addressed at once.
    • Poverty graduation has been tested for nearly two decades. In a recent meta-analysis of 40 randomized trials in 26 countries, graduation programs raised consumption (what a household eats and uses) by about 11%, income by 15% and assets by 40% on average.
  • Unconditional cash transfers, such as GiveDirectly’s, are a popular choice within effective giving. Recent, low-cost graduation programs can be more cost-effective. Earlier, more expensive graduation programs usually were not.
  • Our first recommended charity is: Raising The Village, which runs a two-year graduation program for whole villages in Uganda, Rwanda, the DRC and Tanzania.

  • Our analysis finds Raising The Village to be highly cost-effective. We estimate it delivers the equivalent of doubling one person’s consumption[1] for a year for about $27, which by our calculation is ~6x as cost-effective as GiveDirectly and ~11x GiveWell’s benchmark.

  • Raising The Village aims to grow from serving 1 million people in 2026 to about 2 million in 2027. It can absorb millions in additional funding at the cost-effectiveness we’ve modeled.

Introduction

Hi all, we’re Better Futures Guide, a new charity evaluator focused on livelihoods. We find and recommend nonprofits that reduce global poverty by working with people to increase their incomes and consumption (such as of food, shelter, medical care, and school fees).

We work the way many evaluators do. First, we identify a type of program with a strong evidence base. Then we find well-managed organizations that carry it out in high-impact, cost-effective ways. In practice, that means months of desk research, dozens of conversations with experts, and in-depth discussions with charities on their responses to our questions and data requests. Our recommendations, and the research behind them, are public.

A little about us: Co-founder Rens Bakker worked for nine years at the national government of the Netherlands on labor market and livelihood reforms. Co-founder Elizabeth Weissberg spent fifteen years in research and communications, including at the Aspen Institute and Yale’s Social, Cognitive, and Affective Neuroscience Lab. Aqsa Zaidi, our research fellow, is an MA student at Georgetown with nine prior years of experience in education and development. We’re driven to do this work for many reasons, including that more than 800 million people live on less than $3[2] a day, and that there is strong evidence on how to change that.

This year we focused on three areas within livelihoods: poverty graduation, foundational learning, and cross-border livelihoods. Our first recommendation, below, is in poverty graduation. We’ll share more recommendations as we finish each.

What is poverty graduation?

The premise: address several constraints at once

Poverty graduation is a type of program built on the premise that individuals and families remain in extreme poverty because they face several constraints at once. For instance, a family may have no money to invest, little access to training in farming or business skills, and no savings to absorb a setback, such as a failed harvest or an illness. Graduation programs therefore address these constraints together, typically over one to two years, with the aim that households sustain a higher living standard after the program ends.

Not every graduation program has identical components. However, to be included in the meta-analysis mentioned above, a program combined at least three of these five[3]:

  • A transfer of cash or productive goods, such as tools or equipment, which provides the means to start or expand an income-earning activity
  • Training, for example in farming, livestock care or business skills, to earn more from that activity
  • Consumption support: smaller transfers of cash or food that cover basic needs while the activity becomes established
  • Coaching: recurring visits or group meetings to apply trainings and resolve problems as they arise
  • Savings support, often through a savings group or an account, to build a reserve for emergencies

The approach was pioneered in 2002 and is among the best-evidenced ways to reduce extreme poverty. In a recent meta-analysis of 40 randomized trials in 26 countries, graduation programs raised consumption (what a person eats and uses) by about 11%, income by 15% and assets by 40% on average. Most trials measured effects up to four years after programs ended, and across them consumption gains were on average as large or larger at later measurements.[4] 

Comparison with unconditional cash transfers

Graduation programs and unconditional cash transfers both aim to reduce extreme poverty. Many livelihoods-oriented donors currently give to GiveDirectly, which sends unconditional cash transfers. Depending on a donor's priorities (e.g., immediate freedom of choice), this may be the most values-aligned donation. However, for donors more interested in the size of income or consumption gains per dollar, we think that graduation programs have the potential to be substantially more cost-effective.

Graduation rests on the idea of a ‘big push’ out of extreme poverty: support on several fronts at once, substantial enough for households to raise their living standard durably. That is why programs combine the components described above. In graduation programs started since 2016, the median program cost is about $520 per household, about a third less than earlier programs.[5]

In comparison, unconditional cash typically involves a larger transfer and few or no other components. In GiveWell’s model of GiveDirectly’s Cash for Poverty Relief program, the transfer itself is about $865 to $1,100 per household (2024 US dollars), depending on the country.[6] Because households consume most of the transfer in the first year, about 42-45% of the consumption gain to recipients falls in the first year, and 68-70% within three years.[7] In contrast, our model of Raising The Village’s graduation program shows gains that are more evenly spread and longer-lasting.

In practice, some graduation and cash programs are starting to look more alike. Graduation programs are becoming lower-cost and more similar to cash transfers, while GiveDirectly is experimenting with incorporating aspects of the graduation approach. In graduation programs, the main transfer is now most often a lump sum of cash rather than a physical asset such as livestock, and costs have fallen as implementers sought lower-cost designs and governments took programs on. GiveDirectly, for its part, now pairs its cash transfers with light-touch coaching and savings support. It is also testing whether adding training and behavioral support to large transfers can match graduation programs at lower cost.

The academic literature suggests that recent graduation programs can be more cost-effective than unconditional cash transfers, provided the costs are low. The aforementioned meta-analysis[8] found that graduation typically outperforms cash when looking at programs started since 2016, but usually not in earlier cases, when programs were more expensive. Two earlier meta-analyses found that graduation programs or graduation-inspired additions to cash programs lead to larger impact than unconditional cash transfers, but that this is cost-effective compared to unconditional cash transfers only in specific circumstances.[9]

Overall, we think graduation programs that are well designed, well run and low cost have the potential to be substantially more cost-effective than unconditional cash transfers.

Our recommendation: Raising The Village

As mentioned above, graduation programs differ in cost and in results, so the impact of a donation depends on which organization receives it. Raising The Village runs an unusually low-cost version of poverty graduation. Yet, as we discuss below, a randomized trial found its effects on par with higher-cost programs, and in the meta-analysis referenced above, its trial had the highest benefit-cost ratio of 43 program arms.[10],[11] As we also discuss below, it met our other criteria for a recommendation: it has substantial room for more funding, has sound organizational capacity, and was able to provide us with the detailed cost and monitoring data our evaluation required.[12]

Description of activities

Raising The Village works in remote farming villages in Uganda, Rwanda, the DRC and Tanzania. These villages have few roads, clinics, or other services, and families rely on what they grow for both food and income. Even just after harvest, more than half of households live on less than $3 per person per day (PPP). Its program is structured as follows:

  • Pre-planning. Raising The Village selects villages in coordination with the local government. Its staff then map and survey households, ask the village to list its needs, and select seed packages for later distribution based on local climate data and meetings with households.
  • Core implementation (months 0–6). Households receive the seed packages, and the village receives shared farming equipment, such as a milling machine, spray pumps, water drums, wheelbarrows, and other tools. Households attend training sessions covering topics such as agricultural practices, savings groups, and budgeting. The village elects volunteer committees who receive extra training on a specific topic, mentor their peers, and look after shared equipment.
  • Transition (months 7–12). Each quarter, independent data collectors survey a sample of households to check whether at least 90% are using the practices they were trained in. Villages below that level receive extra training and support. Committee members visit every household on a fixed schedule to provide their peers with support.
  • Community ownership (months 12–24). Volunteer committees take over more of the day-to-day work, such as mentoring neighbors and managing shared tools. Staff shift from delivery to mentoring and then handover, providing refresher trainings where the data show a need. At month 24, the village graduates.
  • Follow-up (months 25–60). Program activity ends. To inform future program design, Raising The Village surveys a sample of households each year until five years after the start of the program to track metrics including income, production, assets, and food security.

Most graduation programs target the poorest households in a village. Raising The Village instead works with every household, and actively involves community volunteers in its programming. According to its theory of change, this provides multiple benefits simultaneously:

  • New practices spread. New practices – e.g., for increasing yields or saving money – spread through the community via shared learning and peer accountability.
  • Downsides of household targeting are bypassed. The program does not have to select households within a community in which even better-off households tend to be poor. Selecting households can be costly, error-prone, and perceived as unfair.
  • Costs are lower. Training can be given to groups, volunteers can mentor neighbors, and no money is spent on deciding which households are eligible.

Raising The Village reached 647,000 people in 2025, 1 million in 2026, and aims to reach about 2 million in 2027. As it grows, it is testing how the program performs in new settings and with new partners. In Rwanda and the DRC, it is currently running deliberately small programs, which it calls Learning Hubs. In Tanzania, its activities launched this year.

Impact

The program has been independently evaluated in a randomized controlled trial (Mahmud and Riley, 2026).[13] The researchers randomly assigned 335 villages and surveyed 3,852 households. About three years after the program began, the trial found the following economic effects in program villages:

These gains showed up in daily life. In the lean season, 25% of households in villages without the program said a child had gone to bed hungry during the past month. In program villages, it was 4%. For adults, the figures were 38% and 6%.

As part of our evaluation, we built a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) of Raising The Village: a model that estimates the impact of a donation made in 2027 or 2028 relative to its cost.   • Cost. We take Raising The Village’s projected cost per participant in 2027–28 in each of its four countries, adjusted upward because, across organizations in general, actual costs tend to exceed projections.

What is poverty graduation?

The premise: address several constraints at once

Poverty graduation is a type of program built on the premise that individuals and families remain in extreme poverty because they face several constraints at once.   • A transfer of cash or productive goods, such as tools or equipment, which provides the means to start or expand an income-earning activity

  • Coaching: recurring visits or group meetings to apply trainings and resolve problems as they arise

The approach was pioneered in 2002 and is among the best-evidenced ways to reduce extreme poverty. Graduation programs and unconditional cash transfers both aim to reduce extreme poverty. Many livelihoods-oriented donors currently give to GiveDirectly, which sends unconditional cash transfers. item.title: $1,000 Giving Summit: Breaking Out of the EA Bubble
item.description:
Published on November 17, 2026 4:48 PM GMT

On December 7–8,  Yield & Spread is hosting The $1,000 Giving Summit, a free, two-day podcast style event bringing together more than 15 influential voices from the personal finance and charitable giving communities to discuss how to make generosity a permanent part of our financial plans.

To my knowledge, this is the first time that this many personal finance pros have come together around this topic. 

The goal is to introduce a mainstream personal finance audience to the ideas of effective giving.

Why now?

Starting in 2026, Americans who take the standard deduction can deduct up to $1,000 in qualifying charitable contributions ($2,000 for married couples filing jointly). Previously, charitable deductions were only available to those who itemized, meaning the tax benefits of giving largely went to wealthier households or those willing to navigate the complexities of itemizing their deductions.

With roughly 90% of Americans taking the standard deduction, this creates a timely opportunity to get more people thinking about charitable giving.

We want to use this tax change as a starting point for a much bigger conversation about generosity, particularly within the Financial Independence world, where people already think deeply about building wealth but don't always talk about what they can do with it.

Who's speaking?

We're bringing together some of the biggest names in personal finance, including:

Mr. Money Mustache: He’s donated hundred of thousands of dollars to GiveWell
Money with Katie: She donates ⅓ of her podcast proceeds to charity
Jim Dahle of The White Coat Investor: 10% pledge-taker
Frank Vasquez of Risk Parity Radio: Also 10% pledge-taker!

They're joined by experts in charitable giving and research, including:

Carolien Teti of GiveDirectly:  They’re offering a 1.5x match as part of the summit
James Rayton of Giving What We Can:  The Index Funds of Giving 
Lara Aknin of the World Happiness Report: Does giving actually make us happy?
Larissa MacFarquhar, author of strangers drowning: Just because she is so influential to me and it was absolutely incredible to interview her :)

There will also be a bonus live Q&A with Financial Planner Cody Garrett who will answer financial planning and tax questions so people can get the help they need asap. 

Together, the speakers will explore everything from how much we can comfortably give and how generosity affects our financial independence plans, to why some charities can accomplish dramatically more with the same donation.

Who is this for?

  • You’re pursuing financial independence and want your money to mean more
  • You want to give more but worry about what it’ll mean for your future
  • You take the standard deduction and want to make the most of the new tax break
  • You itemize but want smarter strategies for charitable giving
  • You want to make generosity a regular value, not just a year-end decision
  • You’re interested in investment strategies that align with pledge-taking and giving meaningful sums of money away

What are we hoping to achieve?

This is an exploration in expanding the top of the funnel for effective giving. Our primary goal is to introduce more people to effective giving and, importantly, turn that awareness into actual donations.

We'll measure success through three key metrics:

  1. The $1,000 Giving Challenge: How many people participate and make a donation they otherwise wouldn't have made. Plus, how many people self-report that they give to more effective charities.
  2. The GiveDirectly Match: How many people participate in the matching opportunity (1.5x), and how much funding does it generate?
  3. The FI-lanthropy Pledge (in partnership with Giving What We Can): How many listeners take the 10% pledge or Trial pledge. We plan to follow up with participants and offer free one-on-one calls to explore making a longer-term giving commitment.

We recognize that self-reported donations won't provide a perfect measure of counterfactual giving, but we hope these results will help us understand whether this type of outreach can encourage more effective generosity when we widen the target to a new audience. 

The summit is free and takes place December 7–8. You can learn more and sign up here.

What this is not

This event is meant to broaden the personal finance world’s exposure to high-impact giving, using language that speaks to them. So we are leading with a carrot, not a stick.

  • We are not excluding people who have charitable interests outside of EA. We are working to expose them to these ideas by bringing their favorite personal finance pros into one space that highlights high-impact giving.
  • We are not positioning effective giving as an all-or-nothing decision. Even small steps toward more impactful giving are worth celebrating at this top of the funnel event.
  • We are not trying to turn the personal finance community into the EA community. We're introducing a new conversation and giving people tools to explore it on their own terms.

We are meeting people where they are at, celebrating progress (not perfection), and creating curiosity. 

Give me your thoughts!

For those of you who have worked on top of the funnel strategy and expanding your reach beyond the center of the target (the existing EA community) - what do you like? What would you change? 

About Me

I’m the founder of Yield & Spread, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that teaches people to build wealth and give it with purpose. I created the FI-lanthropy Pledge, in partnership with Giving What We Can. I’ve helped hundreds of people with their personal finances and giving plans. Yield & Spread has received grant funding from the CEA, and is using part of this funding to support this summit.

item.title: Fish Welfare Initiative’s Funding Gap
item.description:
Published on November 18, 2026 6:44 AM GMT

Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) works to improve the lives of farmed fish as much as possible. We currently operate in India and China, and are considering expanding to a third country in 2027. We work with species and in contexts where there is little prior welfare research, and so we invest significantly in developing new interventions to suit these contexts.

We now have a relatively large funding gap for 2027 (about $500K of our $1M budget). The rest of this post outlines our work in further detail, and also includes our best case against donating.

If you are interested in supporting our work, feel free to reach out or leave any questions below. As always, we also value feedback from the EA community—we’d love to hear which parts of our strategy seem strong, or which parts seem like they have gaps. Thank you!

About Fish Welfare Initiative

For those who aren’t familiar with FWI, the following are the main things to know:

  • What We Do: We work to improve the welfare of farmed fish, who, like other animals, suffer significantly under modern farming conditions. Our interventions to date have primarily focused on improving water quality.
  • How We Do It: Compared to most animal advocacy organizations, we believe our programs are unusually “on the ground”—we visit fish farms every day to conduct research and work with farmers to make improvements. We also have a particular focus on developing new interventions, given the novelty of this field.
  • Where We Work: We operate in Asia, because this is where about 90% of farmed fish live. To date, we have mostly focused on India, though also with smaller projects in China and the Philippines.
  • Where We Came From: Our illustrious founders, Tom and Haven, took part in the first round of the Charity Entrepreneurship Incubation Program, back in 2019. We were both EA student organizers before that, and have no doubt that FWI would not exist if not for the EA community.

You can get more into the weeds of our organization on our website and our blog.

Our Track Record

Since launching in 2019, we have spent about $3.5M, largely received from donors who would have counterfactually given to other very promising opportunities (this is why we try to be mindful about only raising what we need). In this time and with this money, we believe our key accomplishments have been the following:

  • Direct Impact: We estimate that we have improved the lives of 5.3M fish*, primarily through water quality improvements via our farm program in India.
    • *Note that the magnitude of the welfare benefit to these animals remains somewhat uncertain—we are currently seeking to build a welfare measurement team to address this.
  • Intervention R&D: We have conducted various studies over the years to inform interventions to improve farmed fish welfare. For instance, our recent Sentinel Poles study found a promising way for farmers to detect and treat fish lice earlier, and we are now testing it in a multi-month controlled trial. We primarily do these studies to develop better interventions for our own programming, but also hope that other organizations might some day take up our interventions.
  • Progress in China: Over half of the world’s farmed fish live in China—it is by far the most important country, and among the most complex, in the fish welfare space. While we haven’t run on-the-ground programs in China as we do in India, working with our Chinese partners we have contributed to several firsts (to our knowledge) for fish welfare in the country:
    • China’s first industry report on fish welfare
    • China’s first Aquatic Animal Welfare Forum, which we now co-host regularly
    • China’s first fish welfare standards, which we supported in being developed
  • Movement Support and Indirect Effects: While these should be considered secondary to our more direct outputs, we believe we have also played an important role in building the broader aquatic animal welfare ecosystem. For instance, it is our understanding that our input played an important role in nudging Shrimp Welfare Project to explore corporate advocacy (efforts which later became their Humane Slaughter Initiative), and in launching Scale Welfare and later shaping its strategic direction (e.g. the choice to operate in Vietnam and the Philippines).

Our Latest Plans

We are currently finalizing our next strategic plan, which will shape the direction of our work for the next 3 years. So while we are still finalizing some aspects, the following are the main components of what we are planning:

  • International Expansion: We are now planning to expand beyond India and China, and will likely add a third country of operation in 2027. Depending on our success and capacity, further countries may be added later. We intend to continue focusing on Asia, and our primary contenders right now are the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand.
  • Program Growth in India: We plan to expand our farm program in India: in 2027 in our current state (Andhra Pradesh), and to an additional state in 2028. We aim to reach roughly 1,200 farms by 2029 with this expansion (we currently have 195 enrolled in our program).
  • China: We expect our China work in 2027 to focus on developing new interventions with local partners, and on longer-term field building efforts. Further plans are still in development.
  • Continued Applied R&D in India (and other countries): We’ll keep developing new interventions, both through our own studies (e.g. our Sentinel Poles study to address fish lice) and, new for us, by funding others through requests for proposals (RFPs)—starting with our current India RFP and a regional Asia RFP in early 2027. We’ll also scope a new Indian state and new species to learn where interventions are most needed.
  • New, “Systems Change” Style Interventions: We are also exploring investing in indirect, longer-term ways of helping fish. Examples here include corporate outreach, policy work, and supporting other organizations who want to work on fish welfare (e.g. we are considering an on-site “fish welfare fellowship” to train other organizations on how to work with farmers). We are particularly excited about curriculum change—adding fish welfare to the curriculum at fisheries universities and research institutes in India.

Current Funding Gap

We are still in the process of finalizing our 2027 and onwards budgets. However, you can see a preliminary version of them here.

To execute our plans for 2027, we estimate that we will need about $1M. We currently have about $500K raised for 2027, so that puts us at a $500K funding gap for next year (and more for future years). We plan to apply to the usual EA sources, particularly the EA Animal Welfare Fund, to fill part of our gap. However, given the size of our gap, we do think that now is a particularly important time for those interested to donate.

What level of funding would buy different outcomes?

Of course, the reality is that all unrestricted donations go into our general operating budget, but the following are some examples of what different outcomes roughly cost for us to attain:

  • $10: On average, our farm program helps about 10 fish per dollar, so $10 spent on the program helps about 100 fish.
  • $600: A year of water quality monitoring and corrective actions on one farm.
  • $50K: A year of our new Welfare Measurement team, which runs welfare assessment studies on farms inside and outside our program to improve how we measure our impact.
  • $100K: One round of our requests for proposals, funding outside researchers to develop new fish welfare interventions.
  • $125K: A year of Global Growth: scoping new countries in Asia and, if we decide to go ahead in mid-2027, setting up in a third country.
  • $250K: A year of our China work: working with local partners on developing fish welfare improvements, and promoting fish welfare within industry and academia.
  • Beyond our $500K gap: Extra funding would go toward 2028, when we plan to grow in our first new country and expand the farm program into a second Indian state (expected budget about $1.1M).

If you’d like to learn more about donating, see our Donation Page FAQ.

Arguments Against Donating

The following are what I (Haven) currently consider to be the best arguments against donating to our work:

  • Lack of Positive Study Results from R&D Work: Over the past few years, we have run various studies to develop new interventions—specifically on feed fortification, satellite-based water quality monitoring and “chill kill”. We believe that these have been, for the most part, well-run studies, and if there were results to be found, we would have found them. However, to date, most of them have returned negative results (e.g. our feed fortification study surprisingly found no significant welfare benefit of our fortified feed). Our Sentinel Poles study on fish lice is the main exception so far, though it still needs to hold up in a controlled trial. As many of our plans rely on developing new and improved interventions, in India and abroad, this is reason for caution.
  • Cost-Effectiveness: While we believe our programmatic cost-effectiveness is good (our farm program helps about 10 fish per dollar) and is likely among the best in the world in the fish welfare space, it is still lower than what some organizations working on other animals, such as shrimp or chickens, estimate for their own work. For this reason, donors interested primarily in present cost-effectiveness may wish to give elsewhere.
  • Novelty of the Fish Welfare in Asia Space: Farmed fish welfare in Asia is still a very young field. There is extremely sparse research on the welfare issues, and interventions, that affect these animals (this is partly why we invest so heavily in R&D). As a result, much of our work is exploratory and you should likely expect a higher failure rate than in more established areas (e.g. cage-free work to benefit egg-laying hens).

A Note of Gratitude

As always, we’d like to note that most of what we’ve been able to accomplish would not have been possible without the incubation, funding, and staff that the EA community has provided. We are extremely grateful for this community, and it continues to be an honor and a pleasure to be a part of it.
